histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.front: What are the three layers of the skin?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.back: The epidermis (keratinised stratified squamous epithelium), the dermis (connective tissue), and the hypodermis (subcutaneous fat).

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.front: What type of epithelium forms the epidermis?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.back: Keratinised stratified squamous epithelium.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.front: What are the functions of the skin?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.back: Barrier/protection, thermoregulation, sensation, vitamin D synthesis, and immune defence.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.front: How does thick skin differ from thin skin?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.back: Thick skin (palms/soles) has a very thick epidermis with a stratum lucidum and no hair follicles; thin skin (elsewhere) is thinner, has hair follicles and lacks a lucidum.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.front: List the epidermal layers from deep to superficial.
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.back: Stratum basale, spinosum, granulosum, lucidum (thick skin only), and corneum.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.front: What characterises the stratum basale?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.back: A single layer of dividing stem cells (keratinocytes) attached to the basement membrane by hemidesmosomes; it also contains melanocytes and Merkel cells.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.front: What characterises the stratum spinosum?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.back: Several layers of 'prickle cells' joined by desmosomes; it contains Langerhans cells.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.front: What characterises the stratum granulosum?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.back: Cells containing basophilic keratohyalin granules and lipid-rich lamellar granules (waterproofing); the cells begin to die here.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.front: Where is the stratum lucidum found?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.back: Only in thick (palmoplantar) skin, as a clear layer just beneath the stratum corneum.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.front: What is the stratum corneum?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.back: The superficial layer of dead, flattened, anucleate keratin-filled corneocytes that forms the protective barrier.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.front: What is the epidermal turnover time?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.back: Roughly 30–40 days from basal cell division to shedding at the surface.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.front: What are the four cell types of the epidermis?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.back: Keratinocytes, melanocytes, Langerhans cells, and Merkel cells.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.front: What is the origin and function of melanocytes?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.back: Neural-crest-derived cells in the stratum basale that produce melanin and transfer it to keratinocytes via melanosomes for UV protection.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.front: How is melanin transferred and where is it stored?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.back: Melanocytes package melanin into melanosomes and transfer it to surrounding keratinocytes, where it caps the nucleus to shield DNA from UV.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.front: Do darker and lighter skin differ in melanocyte number?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.back: No — melanocyte numbers are similar; differences reflect the amount, type and distribution of melanin produced.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.front: What are Langerhans cells?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.back: Bone-marrow-derived dendritic antigen-presenting cells in the stratum spinosum (containing Birbeck granules); part of skin immune surveillance.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.front: What are Merkel cells?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.back: Mechanoreceptor cells in the stratum basale that mediate fine/sustained touch.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.front: What are the two layers of the dermis?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.back: The superficial papillary layer (loose CT with dermal papillae) and the deeper reticular layer (dense irregular CT).

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.front: What is found in the papillary dermis?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.back: Loose connective tissue, dermal papillae that interdigitate with the epidermis, capillaries, and Meissner's corpuscles (light touch).

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.front: What is found in the reticular dermis?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.back: Dense irregular connective tissue (collagen and elastic fibres), skin appendages, and Pacinian corpuscles (pressure/vibration).

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.front: What is the hypodermis and its functions?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.back: The subcutaneous layer of adipose and loose connective tissue providing insulation, energy storage and cushioning.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.front: Which receptor detects light touch and where is it?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.back: Meissner's corpuscle, in the dermal papillae (papillary dermis).

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.front: Which receptor detects deep pressure and vibration and where is it?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.back: The Pacinian corpuscle, in the deep (reticular) dermis/hypodermis.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.front: Which receptor detects skin stretch?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.back: Ruffini endings.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.front: Which endings detect pain and temperature?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.back: Free nerve endings.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.front: What is basal cell carcinoma and its behaviour?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.back: The commonest skin cancer, arising from basal keratinocytes; it has a pearly rolled edge and rarely metastasises.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.front: What histological feature characterises squamous cell carcinoma?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.back: Keratin pearls (concentric whorls of keratinising cells); it is UV-related and can metastasise.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.front: From which cell does melanoma arise and how is prognosis assessed?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.back: From melanocytes; prognosis is assessed mainly by Breslow thickness (depth of invasion).

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.front: What are the histological features of psoriasis?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.back: Parakeratosis (retained nuclei in the corneum), acanthosis (thickened spinosum), elongated rete ridges, and neutrophilic Munro microabscesses.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.front: What is spongiosis and which condition shows it?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.back: Intercellular oedema of the epidermis; characteristic of eczema/dermatitis.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.front: Contrast pemphigus and pemphigoid.
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.back: Pemphigus (vulgaris) is intra-epidermal blistering from anti-desmoglein (desmosome) antibodies; bullous pemphigoid is subepidermal blistering from anti-hemidesmosome antibodies.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.front: What causes vitiligo versus albinism?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.back: Vitiligo is autoimmune destruction of melanocytes (patchy depigmentation); albinism is a genetic defect in melanin synthesis (melanocytes present but non-functional).

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.front: What is the pilosebaceous unit?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.back: The functional unit of the hair follicle, its sebaceous gland, and the arrector pili muscle (with an apocrine gland in some regions).

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.front: From what do hair follicles and sebaceous glands develop?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.back: They are epidermal derivatives — down-growths of the epidermis into the dermis.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.front: What are the functions of sebum?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.back: To lubricate and waterproof the hair and skin, with mild antibacterial action.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.front: Which skin lacks hair follicles?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.back: Glabrous (hairless) skin — the palms and soles.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.front: What are the three regions of a hair follicle from surface to base?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.back: The infundibulum (surface to sebaceous duct), the isthmus, and the bulb at the base.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.front: What does the hair bulb contain?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.back: The dermal papilla (vascular connective tissue that induces hair growth) surrounded by the proliferating matrix (with melanocytes).

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.front: What is the role of the dermal papilla?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.back: It is the inductive, vascular connective-tissue core that signals the matrix to grow hair.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.front: What is the hair matrix and what does it do?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.back: The zone of proliferating cells around the dermal papilla that produces the hair shaft; it also contains melanocytes that colour the hair.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.front: What are the three concentric layers of the hair shaft from inside out?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.back: Medulla → cortex (keratin and pigment) → cuticle.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.front: What sheaths surround the hair within the follicle?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.back: The inner root sheath, the outer root sheath (continuous with the epidermis), a glassy (basement) membrane, and a connective-tissue sheath.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.front: Why does hair grey with age?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.back: Because the melanocytes in the hair matrix decline, so less pigment is added to the growing hair.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.front: Name the three phases of the hair growth cycle.
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.back: Anagen (active growth, lasting years), catagen (brief regression), and telogen (rest, followed by shedding).

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.front: Where are hair follicle stem cells located?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.back: In the 'bulge' region at the isthmus, near the insertion of the arrector pili muscle.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.front: What is telogen effluvium?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.back: Diffuse hair shedding when a physiological stress (illness, childbirth, surgery) pushes many follicles synchronously into the telogen (resting/shedding) phase; usually reversible.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.front: What type of secretion do sebaceous glands use?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.back: Holocrine secretion — the whole cell fills with lipid and disintegrates to release sebum.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.front: Where do most sebaceous glands empty?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.back: Into the hair follicle (via the pilosebaceous canal).

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.front: What stimulates sebaceous gland activity?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.back: Androgens — which is why the glands enlarge and sebum increases at puberty.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.front: What is the arrector pili muscle and its innervation?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.back: A slip of smooth muscle from the follicle bulge to the papillary dermis, under sympathetic control.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.front: What does contraction of the arrector pili produce?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.back: Hair erection ('goosebumps') and expression of sebum from the sebaceous gland.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.front: Give examples of sebaceous glands that open directly onto the surface (not into hair).
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.back: Meibomian (tarsal) glands of the eyelid, Montgomery glands of the areola, and glands of the lips.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.front: What is the pathophysiology of acne vulgaris?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.back: Follicular hyperkeratinisation and excess (androgen-driven) sebum, with Cutibacterium acnes colonisation and inflammation, producing comedones, papules and pustules.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.front: What organism is implicated in acne?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.back: Cutibacterium acnes (formerly Propionibacterium acnes).

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.front: What is androgenetic alopecia and how is it treated?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.back: Progressive follicle miniaturisation driven by dihydrotestosterone (DHT); treated with minoxidil and finasteride.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.front: What is alopecia areata?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.back: Autoimmune, non-scarring patchy hair loss, classically with 'exclamation-mark' hairs at the edges.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.front: What is a 'sebaceous cyst'?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.back: A keratin-filled cyst arising from the follicle; most so-called sebaceous cysts are actually epidermoid or pilar (trichilemmal) cysts.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.front: What is hirsutism and a common cause?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.back: Androgen-driven growth of terminal hair in a male pattern in women; commonly due to polycystic ovary syndrome.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.front: What is folliculitis / a furuncle?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.back: Inflammation/infection of a hair follicle (folliculitis) or a deeper follicular abscess (furuncle/boil), often caused by Staphylococcus aureus.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.front: What is a chalazion?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.back: A blocked/inflamed Meibomian (tarsal) gland of the eyelid, forming a painless lid lump (a stye involves the gland of Zeis and is usually acute/tender).

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.front: How do the three modes of glandular secretion differ (with skin examples)?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.back: Merocrine = exocytosis (eccrine sweat); apocrine = apical cytoplasm lost (apocrine sweat); holocrine = whole cell lost (sebaceous gland).

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.front: What signals sebaceous tumours may indicate systemically?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.back: Multiple sebaceous neoplasms can be a marker of Muir–Torre syndrome (a variant of Lynch syndrome).

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.front: What is the difference between vellus and terminal hair?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.back: Vellus hair is fine, short and unpigmented; terminal hair is coarse, long and pigmented (e.g. scalp, beard).

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.front: Why does the outer root sheath being continuous with the epidermis matter?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.back: It provides a reservoir of keratinocyte stem cells that can re-epithelialise the skin after superficial wounds/burns.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.front: What are the two types of sweat gland?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.back: Eccrine (merocrine) sweat glands and apocrine sweat glands.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.front: What is the basic structure of a sweat gland?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.back: A coiled tubular gland in the dermis, comprising a secretory coil and a duct.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.front: Where are eccrine sweat glands found?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.back: Throughout the skin (most dense on the palms, soles and forehead).

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.front: Where do eccrine sweat glands open?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.back: Directly onto the skin surface via a sweat pore.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.front: What is the main function of eccrine sweat glands?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.back: Thermoregulation by evaporative cooling.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.front: What cell types make up the eccrine secretory coil?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.back: Clear cells (secreting watery fluid of water and electrolytes), dark cells (secreting glycoprotein), and peripheral myoepithelial cells.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.front: What is the role of the myoepithelial cells in sweat glands?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.back: They contract to expel the secretion from the secretory coil into the duct.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.front: What does the eccrine duct do to the sweat and why?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.back: It reabsorbs Na+ and Cl-, making the final sweat hypotonic (conserving salt).

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.front: By what mechanism do eccrine glands secrete?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.back: Merocrine secretion (exocytosis), with no loss of cytoplasm.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.front: What is unusual about the autonomic control of eccrine glands?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.back: They are controlled by sympathetic cholinergic (acetylcholine) nerves, unlike most sympathetic targets which are adrenergic.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.front: Where are apocrine sweat glands located?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.back: In the axilla, areola, genital/perianal region, external ear (ceruminous) and eyelid (Moll's glands).

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.front: When do apocrine glands become active?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.back: At puberty, under androgen influence.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.front: Where do apocrine sweat glands empty?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.back: Into the hair follicle (not directly onto the surface).

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.front: What is the nature of apocrine secretion?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.back: A viscous, protein- and lipid-rich fluid that is odourless until broken down by skin bacteria.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.front: Why does apocrine sweat cause body odour?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.back: Skin bacteria metabolise its protein/lipid components, producing odorous compounds (bromhidrosis).

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.front: What autonomic nerves control apocrine glands?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.back: Sympathetic adrenergic nerves.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.front: Which modified apocrine glands produce earwax?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.back: Ceruminous glands of the external auditory canal.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.front: What are Moll's glands?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.back: Modified apocrine glands of the eyelid margin.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.front: How does the sweat test diagnose cystic fibrosis?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.back: In CF the defective CFTR channel prevents chloride (and sodium) reabsorption in the sweat duct, so sweat chloride is abnormally high.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.front: Why is sweat normally hypotonic?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.back: The duct reabsorbs NaCl from the isotonic primary secretion faster than water, leaving a dilute (hypotonic) final sweat.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.front: What is hyperhidrosis and how can it be treated?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.back: Excessive eccrine sweating; treated with topical antiperspirants (aluminium salts) or botulinum toxin, which blocks acetylcholine release.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.front: Why does botulinum toxin reduce eccrine sweating?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.back: It blocks acetylcholine release at the cholinergic sympathetic nerve endings that stimulate eccrine glands.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.front: What is hidradenitis suppurativa?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.back: A chronic inflammatory disease of apocrine-gland-bearing skin (axillae, groin) with occlusion, painful nodules, sinus tracts and scarring.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.front: What is miliaria?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.back: 'Heat rash' caused by blockage of eccrine sweat ducts, trapping sweat and producing an itchy vesicular rash.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.front: What is anhidrosis and a genetic cause?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.back: Absent/reduced sweating causing heat intolerance; a cause is ectodermal dysplasia (with reduced/absent sweat glands).

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.front: Distinguish the openings of eccrine and apocrine glands.
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.back: Eccrine glands open onto the skin surface; apocrine glands open into the hair follicle.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.front: Compare the innervation of eccrine and apocrine glands.
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.back: Eccrine glands are sympathetic cholinergic; apocrine glands are sympathetic adrenergic.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.front: Which gland type is responsible for thermoregulatory sweating?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.back: Eccrine sweat glands.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.front: How does the eccrine duct wall appear histologically?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.back: As a two-layered (stratified cuboidal) darker, more eosinophilic tubule, smaller than the secretory coil.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.front: What is bromhidrosis?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.back: Malodorous body odour from bacterial breakdown of apocrine secretions.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.front: What is Fox–Fordyce disease?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.back: A chronic condition of apocrine duct obstruction causing itchy follicular papules in apocrine-bearing skin.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.front: Why are eccrine glands important in a hot environment or fever?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.back: Their evaporative sweat is the body's main mechanism for dissipating heat and lowering core temperature.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.question: The epidermis is composed of:
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.explanation: The epidermis is keratinised stratified squamous epithelium.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.question: The correct order of epidermal layers from deep to superficial is:
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.explanation: Deep to superficial: basale → spinosum → granulosum → lucidum → corneum.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.question: The stratum lucidum is found only in:
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.explanation: The stratum lucidum is present only in thick skin of the palms and soles.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.question: Cell division in the epidermis occurs mainly in the:
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.explanation: The stratum basale contains the dividing stem cells that renew the epidermis.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.question: 'Prickle cells' joined by desmosomes are found in the:
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.explanation: The stratum spinosum consists of prickle cells connected by desmosomes.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.question: Melanocytes are located in the ______ and are derived from ______.
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.explanation: Melanocytes lie in the stratum basale and are neural-crest-derived; they transfer melanin to keratinocytes.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.question: Melanin protects the skin by:
options: Shielding keratinocyte DNA from UV radiation
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.explanation: Melanin caps keratinocyte nuclei, absorbing UV and protecting DNA from damage.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.question: Langerhans cells are:
options: Dendritic antigen-presenting cells in the spinosum
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.explanation: Langerhans cells are bone-marrow-derived dendritic antigen-presenting cells in the stratum spinosum.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.question: Merkel cells function as:
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.explanation: Merkel cells in the basal layer are mechanoreceptors for fine/sustained touch.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.question: Which receptor detects light touch and lies in the dermal papillae?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.explanation: Meissner's corpuscles in the papillary dermis detect light touch.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.question: Which receptor detects deep pressure and vibration?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.explanation: Pacinian corpuscles in the deep dermis detect pressure and vibration.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.question: The waterproofing lipid of the epidermis is released from:
options: Lamellar granules in the stratum granulosum
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.explanation: Lamellar (membrane-coating) granules in the stratum granulosum release lipid that waterproofs the epidermis.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.question: The two layers of the dermis are the:
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.explanation: The dermis has a superficial papillary layer and a deeper reticular layer.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.question: The hypodermis consists mainly of:
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.explanation: The hypodermis (subcutis) is mainly adipose tissue providing insulation and cushioning.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.question: The commonest skin cancer, arising from basal keratinocytes, is:
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.explanation: Basal cell carcinoma is the commonest skin cancer; it has a pearly rolled edge and rarely metastasises.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.question: Keratin pearls are a histological feature of:
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.explanation: Keratin pearls (concentric keratinising whorls) are characteristic of squamous cell carcinoma.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.question: The prognosis of melanoma is best assessed by:
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.explanation: Breslow thickness (depth of tumour invasion) is the key prognostic factor in melanoma.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.question: Psoriasis characteristically shows:
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.explanation: Psoriasis shows parakeratosis, acanthosis, elongated rete ridges and neutrophilic Munro microabscesses.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.question: Pemphigus vulgaris causes blistering by:
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.explanation: Pemphigus vulgaris is intra-epidermal blistering from anti-desmoglein (desmosome) antibodies; pemphigoid is subepidermal (hemidesmosome).

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.question: Spongiosis (intercellular epidermal oedema) is typical of:
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.explanation: Spongiosis — intercellular oedema of the epidermis — is characteristic of eczema/dermatitis.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.question: The pilosebaceous unit consists of:
options: Hair follicle + sebaceous gland + arrector pili muscle
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.explanation: The pilosebaceous unit is the hair follicle, its sebaceous gland and the arrector pili muscle.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.question: The inductive, vascular core at the base of the hair bulb is the:
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.explanation: The dermal papilla is the vascular connective-tissue core that induces hair growth; the matrix around it proliferates.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.question: The cells that produce the hair shaft are in the:
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.explanation: The matrix (around the dermal papilla) is the proliferating zone that produces the hair shaft.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.question: The layers of the hair shaft from inside out are:
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.explanation: From inside out the hair shaft is medulla → cortex → cuticle.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.question: Hair colour is determined by melanocytes located in the:
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.explanation: Melanocytes in the matrix add pigment to the growing hair; their decline causes greying.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.question: The active growth phase of the hair cycle is:
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.explanation: Anagen is the active growth phase (lasting years); catagen is regression and telogen is rest/shedding.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.question: Hair follicle stem cells reside in the:
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.explanation: Follicular stem cells lie in the bulge at the isthmus, near the arrector pili insertion.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.question: Sebaceous glands secrete by which mechanism?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.explanation: Sebaceous glands are holocrine — the entire lipid-laden cell disintegrates to release sebum.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.question: Sebaceous glands normally empty into the:
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.explanation: Most sebaceous glands empty into the hair follicle via the pilosebaceous canal.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.question: Sebaceous gland activity is stimulated by:
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.explanation: Androgens stimulate sebaceous glands, which is why sebum production increases at puberty.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.question: The arrector pili muscle is:
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.explanation: The arrector pili is smooth muscle innervated by the sympathetic system; it raises the hair and expresses sebum.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.question: Which skin lacks hair follicles and sebaceous glands?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.explanation: Glabrous skin of the palms and soles has no hair follicles.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.question: Acne vulgaris involves all of the following EXCEPT:
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.explanation: Acne results from follicular plugging, excess sebum, C. acnes and inflammation — not melanocyte destruction.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.question: Androgenetic alopecia is caused by follicle miniaturisation driven by:
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.explanation: DHT drives progressive follicle miniaturisation in androgenetic alopecia; finasteride blocks its formation.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.question: Diffuse hair shedding after childbirth or severe illness is:
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.explanation: A stressor synchronises many follicles into telogen, causing reversible diffuse shedding (telogen effluvium).

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.question: A blocked Meibomian gland of the eyelid produces a:
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.explanation: A chalazion is a blocked/inflamed Meibomian (tarsal) sebaceous gland of the eyelid.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.question: Which is an example of a sebaceous gland opening directly onto the surface?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.explanation: Meibomian glands (and Montgomery glands of the areola) are sebaceous glands opening directly onto the surface.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.question: The 'holocrine' mode of secretion means:
options: The whole cell disintegrates to release its product
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.explanation: In holocrine secretion the entire cell breaks down to form the secretion (as in sebaceous glands).

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.question: Alopecia areata is best described as:
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.explanation: Alopecia areata is autoimmune, non-scarring patchy hair loss with exclamation-mark hairs.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.question: Multiple sebaceous neoplasms can be a marker of which syndrome?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.explanation: Sebaceous tumours can indicate Muir–Torre syndrome, a variant of Lynch syndrome (mismatch-repair defect).

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.question: Eccrine sweat glands open:
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.explanation: Eccrine glands open directly onto the skin surface via a pore; apocrine glands open into hair follicles.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.question: The main function of eccrine sweat glands is:
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.explanation: Eccrine glands produce watery sweat for evaporative cooling (thermoregulation).

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.question: Which cells of the eccrine secretory coil produce the watery component of sweat?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.explanation: Clear cells secrete the watery fluid (water and electrolytes); dark cells secrete glycoprotein.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.question: The eccrine sweat duct modifies the primary secretion by:
options: Reabsorbing Na+ and Cl- to make sweat hypotonic
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.explanation: The duct reabsorbs NaCl faster than water, producing hypotonic sweat.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.question: Eccrine sweat glands are controlled by:
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.explanation: Uniquely, eccrine glands are innervated by sympathetic cholinergic (ACh) fibres.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.question: Apocrine sweat glands are found in the:
options: Axilla, groin, areola and external ear
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.explanation: Apocrine glands are restricted to the axilla, groin, areola, external ear and eyelid.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.question: Apocrine sweat glands open into the:
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.explanation: Apocrine glands empty into the hair follicle, not directly onto the surface.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.question: Apocrine glands become functionally active:
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.explanation: Apocrine glands develop and become active at puberty under androgen influence.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.question: Body odour from apocrine sweat is due to:
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.explanation: Apocrine secretion is odourless until skin bacteria metabolise it, producing body odour.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.question: Ceruminous glands (which produce earwax) are modified:
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.explanation: Ceruminous glands of the ear canal are modified apocrine glands.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.question: In cystic fibrosis, sweat chloride is high because:
options: Defective CFTR prevents chloride reabsorption in the duct
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.explanation: CFTR dysfunction prevents duct reabsorption of chloride, so sweat chloride is elevated (basis of the sweat test).

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.question: Botulinum toxin reduces sweating in hyperhidrosis by:
options: Blocking acetylcholine release at cholinergic nerve endings
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.explanation: Botulinum toxin blocks ACh release at the cholinergic fibres supplying eccrine glands, reducing sweating.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.question: Hidradenitis suppurativa is a disease of which glands?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.explanation: Hidradenitis suppurativa is chronic inflammation of apocrine-gland-bearing skin (axillae/groin).

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.question: Miliaria ('heat rash') is caused by:
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.explanation: Miliaria results from obstruction of eccrine sweat ducts, trapping sweat and causing a vesicular rash.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.question: Which secretion mechanism do eccrine glands use?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.explanation: Eccrine glands secrete by the merocrine mode (exocytosis) with no loss of cytoplasm.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.question: The secretory coil differs from the duct histologically in that it is:
options: Larger and paler with myoepithelial cells
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.explanation: The secretory coil is larger, paler and has peripheral myoepithelial cells; the duct is smaller, darker and two-layered.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.question: Which gland type is the true thermoregulator?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.explanation: Eccrine glands provide thermoregulatory sweating; apocrine glands are scent-related.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.question: Compared with eccrine glands, apocrine glands are controlled by:
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.explanation: Apocrine glands are sympathetic adrenergic; eccrine glands are sympathetic cholinergic.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.question: Absent or reduced sweat glands causing heat intolerance is seen in:
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.explanation: Ectodermal dysplasia can feature reduced/absent sweat glands, causing anhidrosis and heat intolerance.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.question: Which statement correctly pairs a gland with its opening?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.explanation: Apocrine glands open into the hair follicle, whereas eccrine glands open onto the skin surface.
